title: Hermann Ebbinghaus and the Discovery of the Forgetting Curve (1885)
explainer: In the 1880s the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus ran himself through thousands of memorized nonsense-syllable lists and measured, using a 'savings' method, how much faster he could relearn material after various delays. The resulting forgetting curve showed that most newly learned material decays within hours to days unless it is deliberately revisited, which is the empirical basis for scheduling review at increasing intervals rather than re-reading once and moving on. A personal 'Learning OS' that schedules spaced review is, in effect, an engineering answer to a finding that is now well over a century old.

title: Niklas Luhmann's Zettelkasten: A Note System That Out-Produced Its Creator
explainer: Starting in the early 1950s, German sociologist Niklas Luhmann built an index-card 'slip box' of roughly 90,000 interlinked notes, each given a unique address so a new idea could branch off an existing one instead of sitting in an isolated folder. He credited the system with enabling his unusually large output (around 50 books and hundreds of articles), and it is the direct ancestor of today's networked note-taking tools. It is a concrete historical example of a personal learning system built from disciplined indexing rather than any particular piece of software.
